title: Questions and question tags
intro: How to ask questions in English: the word order, subject questions and the question tags that you hear all the time.

sections.title: Forming questions
sections.summary: Most questions put an auxiliary verb before the subject. Questions about the subject do not need an auxiliary.

tables.caption: Question patterns
head: type
pattern
example
rows: Do you like tea? Have they arrived?
Is she at home? Where are they?
preposition at the end (usual in speech)

uses: Use do / does / did when there is no other auxiliary in the present simple and past simple.
In subject questions the question word is the subject, so you do not use do: Who lives here? (not Who does live here?).
Wh- words: who, what, which, where, when, why, how, whose.
How can go with an adjective or adverb: how old, how often, how long, how much, how many.

examples.text: What time does the film start?
How long have you lived here?
examples.note: How long asks about a period of time.

mistakes.why: In a subject question there is no auxiliary.
What is the object here, so use does.

checks.question: Make a question: She works in a bank. (Where)
checks.explanation: Use does and the base form.

checks.question: Make a question about the subject: Somebody left a message. (Who)
checks.explanation: No auxiliary in a subject question.

sections.title: Question tags
sections.summary: A question tag is a short question at the end of a statement. You use it to check information or to ask for agreement.
uses: The tag uses the same auxiliary as the statement. If there is none, use do / does / did.
Positive statement + negative tag, negative statement + positive tag.
Falling voice: you are sure and want agreement. Rising voice: you are really asking.
Use a pronoun in the tag: Tom is nice, isn't he?

examples.text: It's a lovely day, isn't it?
You haven't seen my keys, have you?

mistakes.why: There is no auxiliary in the statement, so use do.
A positive statement needs a negative tag.

mistakes.wrong: She doesn't eat meat, doesn't she?
mistakes.right: She doesn't eat meat, does she?
mistakes.why: A negative statement needs a positive tag.

checks.question: Complete: They didn't come, ___ ?
checks.explanation: Negative statement, positive tag with did.
